claims.text: The initial material is a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing Mg-based lightweight high-entropy alloy with minimal intermetallic formation.
The initial material has a finely dispersed, relatively uniform microstructure.
The initial metastable microstructure provides high corrosion resistance.
The initial metastable microstructure provides high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Mg diffusion kinetics during thermal annealing dictate the nucleation and growth of intermetallic compounds.
Slower heating and/or longer dwell times accelerate effective Mg diffusion.
Slower heating or prolonged dwell lowers the energy barrier for Mg diffusion.
Enhanced Mg diffusion increases intermetallic nucleation and growth.
Slow thermal treatment produces a higher intermetallic volume fraction than rapid thermal treatment.
Slow thermal treatment produces a coarser distribution of intermetallic phases than rapid thermal treatment.
The resulting intermetallic compounds disrupt a homogeneous protective passivating surface film.
Disruption of the passivating film decreases corrosion resistance.
Intermetallic evolution and disruption of the surface film decrease high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Rapid thermal cycles better retain the metastable microstructure than slow thermal cycles.
Rapid thermal cycles better retain corrosion and oxidation resistance than slow thermal cycles.
The relevant high-temperature oxidation regime is approximately 800–1100 °C.
NaCl-containing solutions are a relevant corrosive service environment for the proposed comparison.
In reported Mg-Ti-Zn alloys, Ti and Zn in the matrix together with uniformly distributed fine intermetallics promoted a protective surface film and high corrosion resistance.
The slow-versus-rapid annealing comparison can be evaluated by measuring intermetallic phase fraction and size, corrosion current and impedance, and oxidation weight gain.
Failure to observe either greater intermetallic evolution or corresponding environmental-resistance deterioration in slowly annealed samples would falsify the proposed pathway.
